title: This Medical Device Went to Market...
subtitle: And the rest languished. A brief history.
body_html:
It's hard to see the future and not see it get better faster—welcome to my personal pain as a humorist/visionary. There's a problem in American healthcare. I know, which one? I will only write about one tiny part of the problem today.

Today, I present a short history of the problems with medical devices in American medical care. Pharmaceuticals have become a huge industry. They've become a huge industry, not thanks to the free market. Like most things in America, government meddling in the free market makes Pharma such a strange and wildly profitable business. When Medicare and Medicaid were created, the government was denied the ability to negotiate drug prices. This became Medicare Part D. So, unlike everywhere else on earth, drugs cost whatever the manufacturer says they cost. For new drugs on patent at least. And the profitability of something as much money as you can dare to ask for? That can be pretty good. That is to say, top 30 company good. Eli Lily, which makes tirzepedide, clocks in at #13, and is larger than #19 UnitedHealth Group, for example, by market cap).

I have a Event in real life with the people who inspire me at our second annual rapid-acting mental health treatment conference in San Francisco on January 12. Get your tickets here.

Most of American healthcare has been built on that completely bonkers decision, which had the subsequent effects you would imagine. What happens to a drug price… if that drug price can be any price? That price is going to go up.

The average price of a new medicine going to market in 2024 is around $300,000. We subsequently had that Hatch-Waxman Act, which created our generic drug marketplace, which also became wildly profitable for a while and drove down costs in a free market way, but also made the Spectre of drug shortages that we were all dealing with now. This was a deal with the devil. Nobody wanted to kill the goose that laid the golden egg, around which you couldn't negotiate a lower price. This has been nibbled around the edges with the inflation reduciton act, but not by much.

Here's a great podcast about generic drugs and all their problems: Tradeoffs, which, again, I'm only using to set up the argument about medical devices that follows.

To be blunt— drug prices are going to go up forever because they can't be negotiated down? They are a terrible idea for a healthcare system. Because of those ever-escalating drug prices, we created pharmacy benefit managers, who can legally move around kickbacks, which are now a massive part of the American healthcare system. Legal kickbacks around impossibly expensive medicines? Sure. Are you noticing a trend?

If it's a problem with American healthcare, it all leads back to the fact that the government can't negotiate the prices around new drugs, and so the cost of those drugs is just going to get higher. If the only thing that limits the cost of your drug is shame? The leadership of those companies has only so much shame to go around. Shame is not in keeping with the fiduciary duty to their shareholders. Increasing profits is.

It turns out, however, that drugs are not the only way to treat medical problems. Drugs don't do any diagnosing. With our fancy training, physicians make diagnoses and can figure out which drugs and treatments go to which people. Surgeons and other interventional specialists use medical devices to treat medical problems. Often, there are drugs involved as well, but not always. What about those items? What about those services? What about those businesses? As it turns out, even brain surgeons and orthopedic surgeons make only a tiny fraction of what drug companies bring in. Everything gets pushed to the side when drugs can be as expensive as shamelessness allows.

When Medicare and Medicaid were created, they didn't create the same payment model around medical devices — “we will pay anything you care to charge” as we had for drugs. Devices are paid for either as part of a procedure code. There's some math done by the American Medical Association, which owns the process of setting up the conversion factor that counts for all those procedure codes, or they're paid for as part of hospital admission. I'm not saying those things can't be very expensive. God knows that fancy scanners and hospitals can lead to many medical bills. Surgery can be wildly expensive. However, it is not infinitely expensive, which is currently the case with medications. There is an opportunity for cutting costs for a government who might be motivated to do so…AHEM.

In a hospital, we have a way of paying for medical devices. You get admitted to the hospital, and the hospital has to buy the medical device they will use to treat you. Then, they submit a bill to the insurance company, which is often in the government, but sometimes it is an employer plan, and they get paid for doing that. They're going to be negotiating about how much payment changes hands. In 2000, we introduced the new technology add-on payment program, which provided an additional payment, on top of the bundled payment for the medical admission to the hospital, which is based on the diagnosis for which you were admitted, to use something new and better.

There is some math that goes into deciding how much each new technology out on payment will be. Still, Medicare recognized that an incentive was needed to have a new technology get into the hospital if it was better than existing treatment treatments and for life-threatening conditions. The New Technology Add-On Payment (NTAP) program has been remarkably successful at quickly getting these new technologies into care in a hospital setting. I’ve written about it before:

Here.

Here.

Here. (from when I was advocating for Magnus Medical’s SAINT system)

and Here.

To make some boring but important points, this system did not exist until 2024 for inpatient psychiatry, and it still doesn't meaningfully exist for inpatient psychiatry. The NTAP only applies to Medicare using a bundled payment model, and 75% of inpatient psychiatric units use a per-day payment model, not a bundled model. They have the wrong contract to use the NTAP program, so if you want to get new technology into a hospital setting to treat or diagnose psychiatric conditions? Essentially, tough luck. You need guaranteed government pay to make that work, and there are no guaranteed government payers without the NTAP. Using a per diem contract (paying a daily rate, not a bundle rate for the whole admission) means nothing New and Good can come to inpatient psychiatry. Thus, it lagged behind the advances of the ICU and its whiz-bang technologies.

Similarly, there is only a tiny brand new program in the outpatient called TCET setting to bring any of these guaranteed government payments for new and better technologies to the outpatient setting. Which means… There are no good and paid-for technologies in the outpatient setting as it relates to mental health. It’s a slog.

If we don't have a path to payment by the government, and thus we won't get new technology to the market. That's the bottom line. We get new drugs… because there's a guaranteed payment model for those. Nobody has to wonder (if they're an investor) if a drug will get paid for it because we all know the rules. Drugs get paid for, and extravagantly well. Medical devices are a slog and don’t get paid for easily, so if you're going write billions of dollars of investments into companies, it damn well better be selling a drug. Your money is less at risk if you're investing in drugs, and so a lot more money gets invested in drugs.

There's a limited and very new way to get paid to have better technology in a mental health hospital. There's also no way to pay for better technology in the outpatient setting for a mental health condition.

There are ways to get payments for medical devices in the hospital setting as long as you're not treating psychiatric conditions in a psychiatric hospital—the NTAP. This is how we have ECMO, implantable pacemakers, and all the novel stuff.

The Breakthrough Therapies Act would help solve this problem, but it hasn’t passed yet—or the similar H.R.1691—Ensuring Patient Access to Critical Breakthrough Products Act of 2024. Again, these things need to pass a pretty dysfunctional Congress. If you ask for a solution, some of those bills will go a long way. And, as I’ve argued before in this letter to Dr. Oz, they are budget-friendly because devices don’t have infinitely increasing drug prices.

Thank you for reading! Call your congress-human and let them know you support these bills.
